People ask me how much of the industry press I read, and the honest answer is almost none of it, which sounds like a confession and is actually the method. Forty pages a week get published about cross-border payments alone. Nobody with a job reads forty pages. What I do takes ten minutes and it is always the same ten minutes. I skim through the summary and the subheadings, fast, and I am not trying to understand anything yet. I am waiting for one thing to snag. Something that contradicts what I thought last month, or a number that is bigger than it should be. When something snags, I stop skimming and I zoom in on that one paragraph and read it properly, twice. Nine of my ten minutes go on two paragraphs. Everything else I have skimmed through and forgotten on purpose, and I have never once regretted it.

Here is something I wish somebody had told me in my first year, because it took me about three years to work out on my own. A press release is not information. It is an argument, written by the company it is about, and paid for by the same company. So it will point out every number that helps it and it will stay completely silent about the one that does not, and none of that is lying. It is selection. The useful question is therefore never is this true. The useful question is what is missing. If a release gives you growth in percentage terms and never once gives you the absolute figure, the absolute figure is small. If it announces a partnership and does not say what either side has committed to, nobody has committed to anything yet. Read what is there, then make a short list of what a normal person would have mentioned and did not appear. That list is the real story.

The thing nobody tells you about keeping up with an industry is that it is a habit and not an event. I have watched very intelligent people try to do it the other way, which is to save everything for a quiet afternoon that never arrives, and then panic-read four hundred pages the night before a conference. That does not work, and it does not work for a reason. What you need is not the information. You already have most of the information. What you need is the pattern, and a pattern is only visible if you look at the same thing at regular intervals. So mine is fifteen minutes on Monday morning, before anything else, every single week. Same three sources, same coffee. Some Mondays there is nothing. But four or five times a year I come across something in those fifteen minutes that changes what my team does that quarter, and none of those things were ever sent to me by anybody.
